Steps: Chapter one. The steps of an appraisal.

Every cost-benefit analysis, from a flood wall to a rule on lorry brakes, goes through the same steps, and the textbooks and the guidance manuals, the Treasury's Green Book in Britain and the Office of Management and Budget's circular in America, agree on them. First, the options, and the counterfactual: what happens if nothing is built. For the bridge, that is not nothing; it is the ferry, still running, with traffic still growing. Every benefit is measured against that. Second, standing: whose gains and losses count. The Island's travellers count, and so does Bo, who loses his trade; whether a visitor from the mainland counts is a choice, and it should be written down. Third, the impacts, year by year: crossings, minutes, fares, deaths, decibels, and the cost of building. Fourth, a value for each in money. Fifth, discount them to today and add them up. And sixth, move every assumption to see which ones decide the answer, before recommending anything.

Here is the bridge's ledger, the Island's first year of it, in millions of Island dollars. Travellers save time on the 0.84 million crossings they make now: 5.4 million a year at the value of time. They stop paying Bo's fare: 3.4 million. A free, fast bridge makes crossings worth taking that were not worth the ferry: 4.3 million of gains on those. Bo loses his ferry's profit, 1.5 million a year. And the ferry is more dangerous than a bridge: about 0.12 fewer deaths a year, valued at the Island's value of a statistical life. Against that: three years and 300 million of building, upkeep every year, and noise for the homes by the approach road. The next three chapters explain where each of these numbers comes from.
Priced: Chapter two. Valuing what has a price.

Dupuit's answer, drawn. The demand for crossings: the cheaper a crossing, the more people make. Its cost to a traveller is the fare plus the value of the time it takes. On the ferry that is 4 dollars of fare and 8 dollars of time, and the Island makes 0.84 million crossings a year. On a free bridge, eight minutes cost 1.6 dollars, and crossings rise to 1.67 million. The gain to travellers is the area between the two prices, under the demand curve. On the crossings already made, each saves the whole difference: 5.4 million a year in time, and 3.4 million in fares. The new crossings gain less: the first was almost worth taking on the ferry and gains almost the whole saving, the last was barely worth taking even on the bridge and gains nothing. On average they gain half, which is why appraisers call it the rule of a half: 4.3 million.

But the fares are not a gain to the Island. Every dollar of fare a traveller no longer pays is a dollar Bo no longer receives. Bo counts too: he loses his ferry's profit, 1.5 million a year. Add the two, and what is left, 1.86 million, is exactly what the ferry cost to run: the boat's fuel, the crew, the upkeep, resources that can now do something else. That is the rule for every transfer in an appraisal, from fares to taxes: it is a gain to one side and a loss to the other, and it nets out, as long as both sides have standing.

Two more corrections to market prices. A shadow price is what a resource really costs society when its market price says otherwise. A builder who would otherwise have been unemployed gives up much less than the wage to build the bridge. If half the bridge's labour came from idle hands, valued at half the wage, the cost would fall by 30 million, and the net present value would rise from 77 million to 106. Most guidance assumes full employment and does not allow this; it is the first thing a project's promoters ask for. The other correction runs the other way. A public dollar is raised by taxes that distort, so it costs society more than a dollar: Part forty-one's marginal cost of public funds. Norway's guidance has long added twenty percent to every krone of public spending. Applied to the bridge, the net present value falls to 13 million. The bridge is still worth building, but only just.
Unpriced: Chapter three. Valuing what has no price.

Most of what a transport project produces is time, and time has no price tag. The starting point is the wage, what people accept for an hour of work. But an hour of travel is not an hour of work, and studies of how people choose between faster and cheaper trips find they value it at less. America's Department of Transportation values personal travel at half the median hourly household income, and asks analysts to try thirty-five and sixty percent too. Travel on the job is valued at its full cost to the employer. On the Island, the bridge's travellers' time is valued at half a wage of 24 dollars: 12 dollars an hour.

Quiet has no market, but houses do, and a house comes with its noise. Sherwin Rosen's hedonic method, from 1974, reads the price of a characteristic from the prices of the things that carry it. Here are 3,000 house sales on the Island, against the road noise outside each. Fit price on noise, and noise seems to raise prices, by 0.28 percent a decibel. The loud homes are by the coast road, and the coast road runs along the harbour, which people pay to live near. Hold the distance to the harbour and the number of rooms fixed, and each decibel lowers the price by 0.75 percent, close to the 0.7 planted in this simulation. A hedonic price is only as good as the list of everything else that comes with the house. For the bridge's approach road, ten decibels for two hundred homes is a loss of about seven percent of their value.

A beach has no entry price either, but getting there does. In 1947 Harold Hotelling suggested to the National Park Service that the cost of the journey could stand in for a price, and Marion Clawson made it a method. Ten villages on the Island lie at different distances from its beach; each trip costs fuel and an hour or so of time. The farther the village, the fewer visits each resident makes: the line through them is the beach's demand curve, with the cost of the trip as its price. A resident whose trip costs 7 dollars gets the area under the curve above that cost: a surplus of 34 dollars a year. Added over everyone, the beach is worth about 763 thousand dollars a year beyond what people spend reaching it, a number to set against a hotel that would close it.

Some things leave no trace in any market: an Alaskan coast that most Americans will never see. When the Exxon Valdez spilled its oil in 1989, the State of Alaska commissioned a national survey that asked people what they would pay to prevent another such spill: about three billion dollars in all. Exxon's experts attacked the method. A study published in 1993 asked groups what they would pay to keep migrating birds from dying in oil ponds: 2,000 birds, 20,000, or 200,000. The answers: eighty dollars, seventy-eight, eighty-eight. A hundred times the birds, the same money. A panel led by Kenneth Arrow and Robert Solow concluded in 1993 that careful surveys could still be a starting point, if they asked as in a referendum and passed a test that more is worth more. Peter Diamond and Jerry Hausman answered that answers which ignore the scope measure a warm glow, not a value, and that then no number is better than some number. Stated preference is still used, with those tests, and still argued over.
Life: The ferry kills people; the bridge would kill fewer. How is that valued? In 1968 Thomas Schelling pointed out that the question is not what a life is worth, but what a small change in risk is worth to the people who bear it. Take ten thousand people. Suppose each would accept nine hundred dollars a year to bear an extra risk of one in ten thousand of dying that year. Between them they accept nine million dollars, and on average one of them dies. That is the value of a statistical life: no one knows whose. It is a rate of exchange for small risks, measured in what people accept, and not the worth of anyone in particular.

Where do such numbers come from? Mostly from pay. Richard Thaler and Sherwin Rosen, in 1976, asked how much more dangerous jobs pay, other things equal. Here are the Island's workers: the risk of death in each job, and its pay. On the Island the premium is planted: nine hundred dollars a year for each extra death in ten thousand, a value of a statistical life of nine million. Regress pay on risk, and the value comes out at 3.5 million. Abler workers earn more and drift, a little, to safer jobs, so the safest jobs look well paid for reasons that have nothing to do with safety. Hold ability fixed, and the estimate is 9.2 million, close to the truth. But risk itself is measured from a few deaths in each occupation, and noisy, which pulls the estimate towards zero: 6.5 million. Real studies face both problems with fewer cures, which is part of why their estimates range from a few million to more than ten.

Part eighteen opened this Dial. The speed limits raised on rural interstates from 1987 give an upper bound of about 3 million of today's dollars. The Environmental Protection Agency's value, from mostly wage-risk studies, is about 11.5 million, and the Department of Transportation's 13.7. The number moves with the method and the people asked, and the Island's own nine million sits inside the range.

Is a statistical life the same at every age? One answer spreads it over the years left, as a value of a statistical life-year. At the Department of Transportation's 13.7 million for a forty-year-old with forty years ahead, a life-year is worth about 0.59 million. Then saving a seventy-five-year-old with ten years left is worth about 5.1 million, not 13.7. In 2003 an alternative estimate in an environmental analysis cut older people's value by 37 percent. Critics called it a senior death discount, and the budget office told agencies to stop using the adjustment. American agencies use one value for every age; how much an older person's remaining years should count is a question the method raises and cannot settle.
PlayIt: Chapter five. Play it: the minister's budget.

Your turn. The Island's minister of finance wants to raise the top rate of income tax from forty to forty-five percent, on income above a hundred and fifty thousand. You are the scorer. Your data are a survey: 44,154 records, each with a weight saying how many taxpayers it stands for, which gross it up to the Island's 401,580. The survey takes one taxpayer in ten, but one in two at the top, where the money is. About ten thousand people have income above the threshold, and their incomes have a long Pareto tail. The static score is arithmetic: five percent of everyone's income above the threshold, added up: 143 million a year. But taxpayers respond. Part forty-one's dial puts the elasticity of taxable income at about a quarter. What will the higher rate really raise?

Here is what happened in the Island's model. With an elasticity of a quarter, incomes in the top band fall by about 2.2 percent: some effort, some deferral, some income moved into forms the tax does not reach. On every dollar that disappears, the forty percent that was already being collected goes too. The higher rate raises 101 million, about 71 percent of the static score. Emmanuel Saez gave the shortcut in 2001: the ratio is about one minus the elasticity times the Pareto exponent times the tax rate over one minus the tax rate. Here, 0.69. The answer moves with the elasticity: at nought, the static score is right; at about 0.5, the rise raises sixty million; at about 0.9, nothing, and beyond that the top of Laffer's curve is passed. So B. A score that ignores behaviour overstates what tax rises raise and what tax cuts cost, and the size of the error is the dial.
Discount: Costs come first and benefits later, so everything turns on how the future is weighed against the present. A dollar in t years counts as one over one plus r, to the power t. At two percent a year, a dollar in thirty years is worth 55 cents today; at three and a half, 36; at seven, 13. A hundred years out, at seven percent, a dollar is worth 0.1 cents: at that rate, nothing that happens to our great-grandchildren counts for much.

For the bridge, the rate decides. Its net present value falls as the rate rises, because the costs come in the first three years and the benefits over a century. At three percent the bridge is worth 139 million; at three and a half, 77; at seven, it loses 118 million. The rate at which it breaks even, its internal rate of return, is 4.4 percent. Whether the Island builds depends on whether the rate the ministry uses is above or below that, and so the rate is not a technicality. It is the decision.

So governments write the rate down. Britain's Treasury builds it from Frank Ramsey's rule: half a percent for pure impatience, one percent for the risk that some catastrophe makes the future irrelevant, and the growth of consumption, two percent, times how fast the value of an extra pound falls as people get richer, one. Three and a half percent. For long horizons the Green Book steps the rate down: three percent after thirty years, then two and a half, two, one and a half. America's budget office took another view in 2003: money for a project could otherwise have been invested, at about seven percent, or consumed, at about three, so report both. In 2023 it cut the main rate to two percent, from the real yield on Treasury bonds over thirty years, and in February 2025 a new administration rescinded the revision and brought the 2003 rates back. In October 2026, after a review by Mark Freeman and Ben Groom, Britain's Treasury accepted a cut of its headline rate to three percent, the first change in about a quarter of a century. The same bridge passes at one ministry and fails at another.

Why should the rate fall with the horizon at all? Martin Weitzman's argument, from 1998: suppose no one knows whether the right rate for the next centuries is one percent or seven, and each is equally likely. Then the value today of a dollar in t years is the average of the two discount factors, not the factor at the average rate. The seven percent world's factor shrinks so fast that, far out, only the one percent world still counts, and the rate from each year to the next falls towards the lowest possible rate. The average rate from today falls more slowly, the shape the Green Book's steps approximate. And the market's own real rate has moved a long way: the yield on ten-year inflation-protected Treasuries averaged 0.97 percent from 2003 to 2025, below zero in some years and above two in others.
Scoring: A law is scored, not appraised. In America the Congressional Budget Office, since 1975, and the Joint Committee on Taxation estimate what each bill does to the budget; in Britain the Office for Budget Responsibility, since 2010; in the Netherlands the Central Planning Bureau, which even scores the parties' election programmes. Everything starts from a baseline: the budget under current law, projected ten years ahead. A static score is the bill's arithmetic with no one changing anything. The conventional score, the official one in Washington, lets people respond, as the Play it did, while holding the size of the economy fixed. A dynamic score lets output, prices and interest rates move too, and is published alongside for the biggest bills.

The ten-year window is a rule, and rules are gamed. A tax cut costing a hundred million a year, written to expire after eight years, is scored at 800 million. Nobody expects it to expire; if it is extended, as most such cuts are, it costs 1000 in the window and keeps costing after. The individual tax cuts of 2017 were written to expire after 2025, which lowered their score and kept the bill within the Senate's rules; in 2025 Congress made them permanent, and the cost of doing so was scored then.

What does a dynamic score add? An Island toy makes the two forces visible. A tax cut costs one percent of GDP a year, ten percent over the window. Lower taxes raise output a little, up to four tenths of a percent here, and the government taxes some of that: the growth pays back 0.86 points. But the cut is borrowed, and more debt raises interest rates, on all of the government's debt, not just the new: that adds 1.22 points. The dynamic score, 10.36, is higher than the conventional one. Real scores show both forces. In April 2018 CBO put the 2017 tax act at about 1.9 trillion dollars over its window, with growth paying back about 0.6 trillion and higher interest costing about as much again. And in 2025 its dynamic estimate of the House's tax bill was about four hundred billion dollars more costly than its conventional one. Tax cuts can pay for part of themselves; at today's debt, the interest can take it back.

How good are the scores? CBO publishes its own record, and the Data Room has every baseline since 1984. Once the effects of laws passed later are taken out, its projection of the deficit for the year it is in misses by 0.5 percent of GDP on average; six years out, by 2.0 points; eleven years out, by 2.3. The white dots are the root mean squared errors, a little larger. The biggest misses are not CBO's economics but the laws. In May 2001 it projected a surplus of 5.7 percent of GDP for 2011. Two rounds of tax cuts, two wars, a drug benefit and a stimulus later, the same projection with the new laws would have been a deficit of 5.0 percent. The actual deficit, after the financial crisis, was 8.4. A baseline is a projection of current law, and current law changes.
Microsim: A tax law changes thousands of households in thousands of ways, and the only way to know who gains is to compute it for each. Guy Orcutt proposed simulating an economy one household at a time in 1957. A microsimulation model takes a household survey, computes each adult's income tax under the rules, adds the child benefit, works out the means-tested credit, which is withdrawn as earnings rise, and arrives at each household's net income, before and after a reform. The Island's survey has six thousand records; their weights gross them up to 176,920 households and 424,505 people, paying 1.69 billion of income tax a year. Every total in what follows is a weighted sum.

The output that ministers ask for first is the distribution table. Suppose the Island raises the tax-free allowance from fifteen to eighteen thousand: popular, and simple. It costs 114 million a year. Ranked by household income and cut into tenths, the poorest tenth gains nothing at all: its members earn too little to pay income tax in the first place. The middle gains most as a share of income, about 2 percent, and the richest tenth gains most in money, 991 dollars a household, but least as a share. A reform described as help for low earners passes the lowest earners by; only the table shows it.

Now pay for it. A top rate of forty-five percent on income above eighty thousand brings the net cost down to 17 million a year, before anyone responds; the Play it showed how much less it would raise once they do. The bottom eight tenths keep almost all their gain. The richest tenth loses 2.8 percent of its net income on average, and 75 percent of its households are worse off. Real models run the same arithmetic on real surveys and real rules: NBER's TAXSIM for American taxes, EUROMOD for every country of the European Union, the Institute for Fiscal Studies' TAXBEN in Britain, and the distribution tables of the Joint Committee on Taxation and the Tax Policy Center. The arithmetic is the easy part; the survey's weights, its missing rich and its under-reported benefits are where the work is.
CGE: Scores and appraisals mostly look at one market at a time. General equilibrium looks at all of them, and its bookkeeping is Part three's social accounting matrix. Here is a small one for the Island: two industries, food and manufactures; two factors, labour and capital; a household that owns both; and a government. Each column pays the rows: the household's column buys food and manufactures, the industries' columns pay labour and capital, the factors pay the household. Every account balances: what each receives, along its row, equals what it pays, down its column. Food uses more labour; manufactures use more capital. A computable general equilibrium model is this matrix made to respond: prices move until every market clears again.

Now tax manufactures at ten percent and hand the revenue back. In general equilibrium, people buy fewer manufactures, 58.5 instead of 60.8, and more food. Food needs more labour per unit, so labour moves into food, and the wage rises by 1.9 percent against the return to capital. Arnold Harberger's insight of 1962: a tax on one industry tends to fall on the factor it uses most, wherever that factor works, and here that is capital. The loss to the economy, the deadweight loss, is 0.20 billion, against 11.2 of revenue. Harberger's partial-equilibrium triangle gives 0.23: the right order of magnitude, a little high, because the triangle takes the supply of manufactures as flat, while in general equilibrium the factors cannot leave without their prices changing, so output falls less. For a small tax, the triangle is enough; for a large change, the economy-wide model earns its keep.

Such models are used to score trade agreements, and they can be checked afterwards. Before the North American Free Trade Agreement took effect in 1994, the leading applied general equilibrium models predicted how trade would change, industry by industry. A decade later Timothy Kehoe compared their predictions with what happened. They had drastically underestimated how much trade would grow, and their predictions for each industry were roughly uncorrelated with the outcomes; the biggest growth came in goods that had hardly been traded before, a margin the models did not have. The lesson is the same as for every forecast in this series: a model's structure is a forecast too, and it should be scored.
Risk: Chapter ten. Risk, optimism and the record.

Every number in the bridge's appraisal is a forecast, and forecasts of public works have a record. Bent Flyvbjerg, Mette Skamris Holm and Søren Buhl collected 258 transport projects worth ninety billion dollars. Nine in ten cost more than forecast. In constant prices, rail projects came in 45 percent over on average, bridges and tunnels 34 percent, roads 20 percent, with long tails. Their forecasts of rail passengers were 106 percent too high on average: twice the riders that came. The Channel Tunnel ran about eighty percent over budget. They asked whether this was error or lie. Errors would cancel out; these do not. Part is optimism, the planning fallacy of Daniel Kahneman's work; part, they argued, is strategic: an honest estimate loses the competition for funds.

The cure Kahneman proposed is the outside view: before trusting the inside story of this project, ask how projects like it turned out. The Island has a record: its last sixty public works, each a dot at its outturn cost over its forecast, planted to match Flyvbjerg's averages. 70 percent came in over budget; the median overrun was 14 percent, and one project in five overran by more than 53. Britain's Treasury tells appraisers to raise their cost estimates for optimism bias, and its transport department takes the uplift from the reference class. Uplifted to the eightieth percentile, the bridge's net present value at three and a half percent is minus 76 million. Run the appraisal four thousand times, with costs and traffic drawn from the record, and its forecast of plus 77 million becomes an average of minus 40, with a 61 percent chance of losing money. The bridge that passed on its own forecasts fails on the record of forecasts like them.

Uncertainty has a second consequence. A bridge cannot be unbuilt, so waiting has a value, Part twenty-three's option to wait. Suppose that a year from now the Island will know whether traffic will be thirty percent above the forecast or thirty percent below. Build now, and the expected net present value is 77 million. Wait, and build only if traffic turns out high: 93 million, even after a year's delay. The option is worth 16 million. If costs run twenty-eight percent over, as the record suggests they will, building now is worth minus 4, and waiting 54: the option to wait is worth 58 million, more than the bridge itself. Irreversible decisions under uncertainty should be taken later than a simple net present value says.

The other half of the record is evaluation after the fact, when the outcomes are known. Part forty-two's marginal value of public funds puts that on one scale. Nathaniel Hendren and Ben Sprung-Keyser scored 133 American policies, from what their beneficiaries would pay for them and what they really cost the government, long-run taxes included. Spending on children's health and education came out highest, and much of it paid for itself. Policies for adults mostly delivered between 0.5 and 2 dollars of value per dollar of net cost. An appraisal is a forecast; an evaluation is the score. Governments that commission both, and compare them, learn which of their forecasts to trust.
Rules: Laws are scored; regulations are appraised. In February 1981 Ronald Reagan's Executive Order 12291 required American agencies to analyse the costs and benefits of every major rule, and not to proceed unless the benefits outweighed the costs, with an office in the budget office to check. In 1993 Bill Clinton's Executive Order 12866 replaced it, asking agencies to choose the approach that maximizes net benefits, counting what cannot be quantified too, and every president since has kept its core. Circular A-4 is the manual: the baseline, the alternatives, the discount rates of the last chapter, and how to report uncertainty.

Here is one on the Island. The ministry proposes scrubbers at its two power stations: sixty million to install, forty a year to run, for twenty years. The benefits: about 4 fewer deaths a year from cleaner air, at a value of a statistical life of 9 million, and a little less carbon, at a social cost of 120 dollars a tonne. At two, three and seven percent the rule passes, by 71, 59 and 25 million. With a value of a statistical life of five million, it fails at every rate. When a benefit is hard to value, the honest report is a break-even: the rule is worth it if it prevents more than 3.6 deaths a year. A reader who doubts the epidemiology can then judge the one number that matters.
Goodhart: Chapter twelve. What targets do to numbers.

Every number in this part is meant to inform a decision, and once a decision depends on a number, people act on the number. Charles Goodhart, an economist at the Bank of England, put it for monetary policy in 1975: any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes. Donald Campbell, a psychologist, put it for social policy: the more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures, and the more apt it will be to distort and corrupt the social processes it was intended to monitor.

England gave its hospitals a target: patients in emergency departments should be admitted, transferred or discharged within four hours, for ninety-eight percent of them from 2005. Here is an Island emergency department before any target: the time each patient spends, with a long tail past four hours. Now set the target, and suppose staff move on most patients who would have breached it by less than two hours, in the last fifteen minutes before the deadline. The share seen within four hours jumps from 79 to 91 percent, and a spike grows just under the line. The typical patient's wait has not changed at all. In England the share waiting over four hours fell from 23 percent in 2002 to 5.3 in 2004. Much of that was real improvement; Gwyn Bevan and Christopher Hood also collected reports of patients moved to wards, or ambulances kept waiting outside, to beat the clock. Every appraisal target, a benefit-cost ratio above one included, invites the same, which is the best argument for scoring forecasts against outcomes.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: the discount rate and cost overruns.

This part opens two Dials. The first is the social discount rate. America's budget office, in 2003, asked for 7 and 3 percent, and does again. Britain's Treasury used 3.5 percent for a quarter of a century and has just accepted 3. The 2023 American revision chose 2, and two hundred experts surveyed by Moritz Drupp and coauthors averaged 2.27, with a median of two. The market's own real rate on ten-year inflation-protected bonds has averaged 0.97 percent since 2003. The status is contested: the number is partly economics, the growth and the risk of the future, and partly ethics, how much later generations should count, and a bridge or a climate rule can pass or fail on it.

The second Dial is how far public works overrun their budgets. In Flyvbjerg, Holm and Buhl's projects, rail ran 44.7 percent over, bridges and tunnels 33.8, roads 20.4, and all of them together about 28. It depends on the setting: on the kind of project, the country and the decade, and on which projects keep good enough records to be counted. But the direction does not depend on the setting. An appraisal that takes the cost estimate at its word is biased towards building.
Frontier: Chapter fifteen. Frontier: weights and wellbeing.

Two questions at the edge of the method. The first: should a dollar count the same whoever gets it? Standard cost-benefit analysis says yes, and leaves the distribution to the tax system. The alternative is to weight each dollar by how much it means to the person who receives it: the median income over theirs, to a power. With the power at one point four, a dollar to a household at half the median counts 2.64 times, and one at twice the median 0.38 times. America's 2023 circular allowed such weights, and the circular was rescinded two years later; Britain's Green Book permits them as a sensitivity. The second question: must everything be turned into dollars at all? Since 2021 Britain's Treasury has allowed appraisals to count wellbeing directly, in WELLBYs, one point of life satisfaction on a scale of ten for one person for a year, valued at 13,000 pounds at 2019 prices, if the effect on wellbeing has been measured by a credible experiment.

Three developments, and what remains hard. Tax and benefit calculators are being published as open code, so that anyone can score a reform and check an official score. Demand forecasts learned from data on many past projects automate Kahneman's outside view, and they too will need a record. And evaluation after the fact is spreading: England's road agency, for one, evaluates its larger schemes a year and five years after they open, against the forecasts that justified them. What remains hard is what this part found hard: values without markets, the rate at which to weigh the centuries, and the behaviour of people who know they are being scored.
